timeline.place: Khwarazm or near Baghdad, Abbasid Caliphate, (Uzbekistan or Iraq)
timeline.title: Born, probably around 780
timeline.text: Almost nothing certain is known about his early life. His name points to Khwarazm, a region south of the Aral Sea, and a later writer gives that as his birthplace. But the historian al-Tabari adds names that suggest a link to Qutrubbul near Baghdad, and to Zoroastrian ancestry. Scholars disagree on all of this.

timeline.title: A new caliph in Baghdad
timeline.text: Harun al-Rashid became caliph in 786. Baghdad was the young capital of the Abbasid Caliphate.

timeline.title: A library of translated books
timeline.text: Around this time, a royal library may have begun under Harun al-Rashid. Scholars in Baghdad were translating Greek, Syriac, Persian and Indian books into Arabic, the learning al-Khwarizmi would later build on. The year here is approximate.

timeline.title: Civil war
timeline.text: Harun died in 809. His sons al-Amin and al-Ma'mun fought a civil war over the throne.

timeline.title: A caliph who loved science
timeline.text: Al-Amin was killed in 813 and al-Ma'mun became caliph. Al-Ma'mun strongly supported scholars, and al-Khwarizmi later praised his love of science in the preface to his Algebra.

timeline.title: At the House of Wisdom
timeline.text: Around 820 he is said to have become an astronomer and head of the library at the House of Wisdom, working near scholars such as the Banu Musa brothers. Historians debate what the House of Wisdom was: a formal academy, a royal library, or a name for Baghdad's circle of scholars.

timeline.title: Tables of the sky
timeline.text: His Zij al-Sindhind, astronomical tables based mostly on Indian methods, covered calendars, the positions of the planets, eclipses and tables of sines. The Arabic original is lost.

timeline.title: The Algebra
timeline.text: Around 820 he wrote a short book on calculating by al-jabr (restoring) and al-muqabala (balancing). He wrote that al-Ma'mun had encouraged him to write it. Its title gave us the word "algebra". Scholars give dates between 813 and 833.

timeline.title: Six standard cases
timeline.text: The Algebra sorts equations into six standard types and gives a step-by-step recipe for each. Everything is written in words, with no symbols: the unknown is a "root" or a "thing".

timeline.title: Proof by picture
timeline.text: For the harder cases he drew a square with strips on its sides to show why his recipe works. This is the method of completing the square still taught in schools.

timeline.title: Maths for daily life
timeline.text: The second half of the book applies the methods to measuring areas and volumes and to dividing inheritances under Islamic law, problems people faced every day.

timeline.title: Counting the Indian way
timeline.text: Around 825 he wrote a book on Indian arithmetic: nine digits plus a sign for an empty place, where a digit's position gives its value. The Arabic original is lost, but Latin versions spread these numerals in Europe.

timeline.title: Measuring the world
timeline.text: Al-Ma'mun built an observatory in Baghdad around 828 and paid for work to measure the Earth's size and draw a world map. Al-Khwarizmi is reported to have taken part, but the details of his role are uncertain.

timeline.title: The Picture of the Earth
timeline.text: He finished his geography, Kitab Surat al-Ard, a revision of Ptolemy's Geography listing the coordinates of 2,402 places. It improved on Ptolemy for lands Arabic writers knew well. One Arabic copy survives, in Strasbourg.

timeline.title: His patron dies
timeline.text: Al-Ma'mun, the caliph who had encouraged his work, died in 833.

timeline.title: Instruments, calendars, history
timeline.text: He also wrote on the astrolabe and the sundial, on the Jewish calendar, and a history book. We do not know when; the year here is only a marker.

timeline.title: A journey north?
timeline.text: Under the caliph al-Wathiq (842 to 847), al-Khwarizmi is said to have joined an embassy to the Khazars. This is not certain.

timeline.title: Death
timeline.text: He probably died around 850. The exact year and place are unknown.

timeline.title: Algebra comes to Europe
timeline.text: Robert of Chester translated the Algebra into Latin in 1145, and Gerard of Cremona made another version. Earlier in the century, his arithmetic appeared in Latin as Algoritmi de numero Indorum, which opens "Dixit Algoritmi", "so said al-Khwarizmi". His Latinised name became the word algorism, later algorithm.

timeline.title: The Algebra in English
timeline.text: Frederic Rosen published the Arabic text of the Algebra with the first English translation, from a manuscript at Oxford.

timeline.title: Remembered by name
timeline.text: A Soviet stamp marked roughly his 1200th birthday in 1983. A crater on the Moon and two asteroids are named after him, and every "algorithm" carries his name.

feature.title: Words and ideas he gave the world
feature.lead: Few people have left so many words in everyday use. Here are the ideas al-Khwarizmi wrote down or passed on, and the words they became.

items.label: Algebra
items.text: From al-jabr, "restoring", in the title of his book. Robert of Chester's Latin translation of 1145 made it a European textbook for centuries.

items.label: Algorithm
items.text: From Algoritmi, the Latin form of his name, at the start of his arithmetic: "Dixit Algoritmi". It became algorism, and in the 1500s algorithm.

items.label: Restoring and balancing
items.text: Al-jabr moves a subtracted amount to the other side; al-muqabala cancels equal amounts on both sides. These two moves are still the first steps in solving equations.

items.label: Six standard equations
items.text: He sorted the problems he needed into six kinds, each with its own recipe, so any problem could be turned into a known case.

items.label: Completing the square
items.text: A drawing of a square with strips added to its sides proves why his recipe for quadratic equations works.

items.label: Indian numerals and zero
items.text: His book on Indian arithmetic explained the place-value system, perhaps with zero as a placeholder. Through Latin versions, Europe learned the digits we now call Hindu-Arabic numerals.

items.label: Maths for inheritance and trade
items.text: He wrote for people dividing estates, trading, measuring land and digging canals. About half the Algebra is worked inheritance problems.

items.label: Tables of sines and stars
items.text: His Zij al-Sindhind brought Indian astronomy into Arabic, with tables for the planets, eclipses and sines. Adelard of Bath put a revised version into Latin in 1126.

items.label: A map in numbers
items.text: His Picture of the Earth listed latitude and longitude for 2,402 places, revising Ptolemy so the world could be redrawn from coordinates.

items.label: Words, not symbols
items.text: He wrote every problem in plain words, with the unknown called a "thing" or a "root". Symbols came centuries later, but his step-by-step style lasted.

works.title: The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing (al-Jabr)
works.text: The first surviving book to treat algebra as its own subject, with six standard equations, geometric proofs, mensuration and inheritance problems. Some historians call it the foundation of algebra; others rate his achievement more modestly.

works.title: Book on Indian arithmetic (Algoritmi de numero Indorum)
works.text: An explanation of calculating with Indian place-value numerals. The Arabic is lost; the Latin versions differ from the original.

works.title: Zij al-Sindhind (astronomical tables)
works.text: Tables for calendars, planets, eclipses and sines, based largely on Indian astronomy. Survives in Latin versions.

works.title: Kitab Surat al-Ard (The Picture of the Earth)
works.text: A geography listing coordinates for 2,402 places, revising Ptolemy. One Arabic copy survives in Strasbourg.

works.title: Works on the astrolabe
works.text: Two works on the astrolabe, an instrument for measuring the positions of the stars and telling time. Dates unknown.

works.title: Work on the sundial
works.text: A work on sundials. Date unknown.

works.title: Treatise on the Jewish calendar
works.text: A study of how the Jewish calendar is calculated. Date unknown.

works.title: Kitab al-Tarikh (history)
works.text: A political history, known from later writers and a fragment. Date unknown.
